clue.text: Busy man in Gretna Green having obsession about college, Keble oddly, leading Scots cause

indicators.note: the wrapped piece leads, so it comes first and the Scots word follows it
the obsession goes about, so it wraps round what follows it
done oddly, the college name is set down in a strange order

parts.note: a bug is a craze or obsession
C is the abbreviation for college
the Oxford college name with its letters rearranged
gar is Scots for to cause or make

explanation.surface: Some busy Gretna Green figure, fixated on an Oxford college, leads a Scottish cause.
explanation.walkthrough: Gretna Green is the Scottish border village where eloping English couples could marry without formalities; Keble is an Oxford college, here only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A buckle-beggar is a Scots term for a hedge-priest who conducted irregular weddings, a busy trade at Gretna Green.

clue.text: Devoted troubadour, one in delicate silk fabric

parts.note: Blondel, the minstrel of legend who searched for the captive Richard I
an ace is a one in cards and dice

explanation.surface: A loyal minstrel dressed in fine silk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container signal, but it only joins wordplay to definition. Legend says the minstrel found the imprisoned Richard the Lionheart by singing outside his castles.
explanation.definitionFit: Blonde lace is a fine bobbin lace made of silk, originally of unbleached, cream-coloured silk.

clue.text: First in Cortina getting round but not on 'gluey' snow

indicators.note: the first piece gets the next one added after it
but not means without, so those letters are dropped
first in a word means only its opening letter is used

parts.note: the opening letter of the ski resort's name
taken as written
these two letters are taken out of round

explanation.surface: A skier in Cortina d'Ampezzo goes round the piste but avoids sticky snow.
explanation.walkthrough: Cortina d'Ampezzo is an Italian ski resort, which sets the snowy scene; 'on' looks like a link word but is the pair of letters removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Crud is skiers' slang for heavy, wet, sticky snow that is hard to turn in.

clue.text: Peckish kestrels may be found devouring such intestines

indicators.note: the phrase is shown devouring the answer, holding it inside its own letters

parts.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: Hungry birds of prey might be seen eating a meal of guts.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the two words: pec(KISH KES)trels.
explanation.definitionFit: Kishkes is a Yiddish word for guts or intestines, also a sausage made in beef casing.

clue.text: Intricate lay about Norman town butterflies

indicators.note: something intricate is twisted and tangled, so its letters are jumbled
the jumbled word goes about the town, wrapping round it

parts.note: the letters of lay rearranged
Caen is a city in Normandy

explanation.surface: A complex old song about a Norman town and its butterflies.
explanation.walkthrough: A lay is a short narrative poem or song, which hides that the word is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Lycaena is the genus of the copper butterflies, small bright orange species.

clue.text: Resinous stuff, curry accompaniment with parts interchanged

indicators.note: the word's two halves change places, the back one moving to the front

parts.note: sambal is a spicy Malay relish served with curries

explanation.surface: A sticky resin is a curry side dish with its parts swapped round.
explanation.definitionFit: Balsam is an aromatic resin that oozes from certain trees, used in ointments and perfumes.

clue.text: Sticky stuff one found in mine brought up

indicators.note: something found in another thing is inside it
in a down entry, bringing a word up means reading it from bottom to top

parts.note: egg is old slang for a bomb or mine
un is a dialect form of one, as in a good un

explanation.surface: Something gooey is dug out of a mine and brought to the surface.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mine' is a noun, a buried explosive, not the possessive; in a down clue 'brought up' turns a word backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Gunge is informal British slang for any unpleasant sticky or gooey substance.

clue.text: Rent traditionally yielded pounds

parts.note: gave means yielded or gave way
l, from Latin libra, is the abbreviation for pounds

explanation.surface: Old-style rent that brought in money for the landlord.
explanation.walkthrough: Gavel here is not the auctioneer's hammer but the old legal term for rent or tribute.
explanation.definitionFit: In old English law a gavel was a payment of rent or tribute due to a lord.

clue.text: Stern critic, air dreadfully formal

indicators.note: something done dreadfully is badly done, leaving the letters in a mess

parts.note: taken as written
starch is stiff, formal manner

explanation.surface: A severe reviewer with a dreadfully stiff and formal air.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristarchus of Samothrace was a famously severe Greek critic of Homer, so his name means any harsh critic.

clue.text: These Georgian coins show some similarity

indicators.note: showing some of a word means only part of it is on display

parts.note: the letters sit inside the middle of this word

explanation.surface: Two sets of Georgian coins look rather alike.
explanation.walkthrough: Georgian here means the country in the Caucasus, not the British period of the four Georges.
explanation.definitionFit: The lari is the currency unit of the republic of Georgia, and its plural form is unchanged.

clue.text: Timber tree universal in Asia or all over the place

indicators.note: one letter is placed in among the other words before they are mixed
letters scattered all over the place end up in a jumbled order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
U is the film-rating abbreviation for universal

explanation.surface: A timber tree found everywhere, in Asia or scattered all around.
explanation.definitionFit: The souari or saouari is a tall South American tree valued for its hard wood and its edible nuts.

clue.text: Production of Aida: no —— is wasted for Ecuadorians?

indicators.note: a production of a work stages it anew, so the letters are put in a new order
letters that are wasted are thrown away, so they come out of the longer word

parts.note: taken as written
the Verdi opera title and the following word, taken as letters

explanation.surface: A staging of Verdi's opera so lavish that no money is wasted on it.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap and AIDA NO plus SUCRE is an anagram of ECUADORIANS; so ECUADORIANS minus the letters of AIDA NO leaves those of SUCRE.
explanation.definitionFit: The sucre was Ecuador's currency until the country adopted the US dollar in 2000.

clue.text: Swallowing drink back the eye endlessly accounts for minor works

indicators.note: the eye word loses its final letter, so it has no end
the outer word swallows the drink, taking it inside itself

parts.note: ocular is a facetious noun for the eye; without its last letter

indicators.note: a drink taken back is written from its end to its start

parts.note: to sup is to drink

explanation.surface: A drink-swallowing eye somehow explains some lesser pieces of work.
explanation.walkthrough: Chambers gives 'ocular' as a jocular noun for the eye, which is why 'the eye' yields a word normally used as an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Opuscula is the Latin plural of opusculum, a small or minor literary or musical work.

clue.text: Pen scrawled these as template for desktop publishing

indicators.note: words that are scrawled are written messily, so their letters come out jumbled

parts.note: a style is a pointed writing instrument, a stylus
the letters of these rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone scribbles notes to use as a page layout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen' looks like the scribbler's tool or a verb meaning write, but stands for its old synonym style.
explanation.definitionFit: A style sheet is a document defining the fonts and layout rules applied to every page of a publication.

clue.text: As reported curia disturbed upper-class house-god

indicators.note: what is disturbed is moved out of place, so the letters change order

parts.note: the letters of curia rearranged
U is the label for upper-class usage
a lar is a Roman household god

explanation.surface: A papal court in disarray, with a household deity of the posh, as told by someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The curia is the papal court; here it is only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Auricular means known by hearing or by report, from the Latin for the ear.

clue.text: Like top savants from generations carved in stone?

indicators.note: something carved in a material sits inside it

parts.note: st is the abbreviation for stone, the weight
ages are long eras or generations

explanation.surface: Pictures the wisest scholars as if their wisdom were set in stone across the generations.
explanation.definitionFit: Savants are learned people; the top ones are the wisest, the superlative of the adjective sage.

clue.text: Diving bird folded wings switching positions

indicators.note: the wings are the outermost letters, and here they trade places with each other

parts.note: rucked means creased or folded up

explanation.surface: A diving bird folds its wings and changes its position on the water.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the first and last letters of RUCKED gives DUCKER. 'Wings' looks like the bird's own, but means the outer letters of a word.
explanation.definitionFit: A ducker is a dialect name for a bird that dives under water, such as the little grebe.

clue.text: Penalty for bouser — vital to gulp litre before time

indicators.note: what gulps something takes it inside itself

parts.note: key means crucial or vital

indicators.note: the litre is placed before the time in the swallowed part

parts.note: l is the abbreviation for litre
t is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A boozer's punishment: someone must be made to gulp a litre against the clock.
explanation.walkthrough: KEY swallows L then T, giving KELTY. A bouser is an old spelling of boozer, a heavy drinker.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots, a kelty is a full glass a drinker is forced to down as a forfeit for not drinking fairly.

clue.text: Academician set out to destroy minority language

indicators.note: someone set out of a group is removed from it

parts.note: to erase is to wipe out or destroy
A stands for academician, as in ARA

explanation.surface: An academic sets out to wipe out a language spoken by few.
explanation.walkthrough: ERASE loses one A, leaving ERSE. A is the Associate's academician letter in ARA (Associate of the Royal Academy).
explanation.definitionFit: Erse is an old name for Scottish or Irish Gaelic, both spoken today by small communities.

clue.text: It's a sedative, except among men all endlessly active

indicators.note: the word loses its final letter, so it runs without an end
one word placed among others goes inside them
letters made active move about rather than staying in order

parts.note: taken as written
the word all without its last letter
but means except, as in all but one

explanation.surface: A drug that calms everyone except the lively men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Active' sits at the end but governs the men and the shortened all together, which are mixed before the exception goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Nembutal is a trade name for pentobarbital, a barbiturate drug used to calm patients and induce sleep.

clue.text: Dub person scornfully 'little Lambert' in gathering

indicators.note: pieces placed in a word go inside it

parts.note: a bee is a social gathering, as in a sewing bee
tit is a scornful word for a foolish person
L is the symbol for the lambert, a unit of brightness

explanation.surface: Calling someone 'little Lambert' at a party to sneer at them.
explanation.walkthrough: Lambert looks like a man's name; here it is the physics unit, and 'little' signals its symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: To betitle is to give a title or name to someone, which is what dubbing does.

clue.text: Illiterate admitting tons to retrace in Shakespeare

indicators.note: what admits something lets it in, so it sits inside

parts.note: unread means uneducated or illiterate
t is the abbreviation for tons

explanation.surface: A person who cannot read lets heaps of words in to trace them over in Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare uses untread in King John, 'We will untread the steps of damned flight', meaning to go back over.

clue.text: It may prevent chaps charged with energy grabbing pals roughly

indicators.note: handled roughly, the letters are knocked out of order
the outer word grabs the other and holds it inside

parts.note: a live wire is charged with electrical energy
the letters of pals rearranged

explanation.surface: Reads as something that might stop energetic men roughly seizing their friends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chaps' looks like men, but here it means chapped skin, the sore cracks on lips in cold weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Lip salve is a balm rubbed on the lips to stop them cracking or chapping.

clue.text: Arab involved in nasty fall flipped over — wallop

indicators.note: something involved in another thing is caught up inside it
something flipped over is turned end to end

parts.note: a purl is a heavy fall or tumble
Ar is the abbreviation for Arab or Arabic

explanation.surface: An Arab takes a nasty tumble and comes down with a thump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nasty fall' is one unit, an old word for a heavy tumble, rather than an anagram signal plus a word.
explanation.definitionFit: To larrup is a dialect verb meaning to beat or thrash, just as wallop means to hit hard.

clue.text: American swagger evidenced in 'helluva pork-barrel'

indicators.note: what is evidenced in a phrase can be seen inside its letters

parts.note: the letters span the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: US political bluster shows itself in a huge pork-barrel spending bill.
explanation.walkthrough: Pork-barrel is American slang for public money spent to win local votes, which fits the boastful scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Vapour, spelt vapor in the US, can mean boastful talk or bragging, and so swagger.

clue.text: Snorter of old Warne bowled, taking wicket

indicators.note: bowled over, the remaining letters are knocked into a new order
taking a wicket removes it, so that letter is taken away

parts.note: Shane Warne, the Australian leg-spin bowler
w is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for wicket

explanation.surface: A cricketing picture: a snorter is also a vicious delivery, and Warne bowled one to take a wicket.
explanation.walkthrough: WARNE without its W leaves ARNE, rearranged to NARE. A snorter in cricket is a fierce, nasty ball, which is the misdirection here.
explanation.definitionFit: Nare is an archaic word for a nostril, the thing one snorts through, hence a jocular snorter.

clue.text: Showy male goes without PE defiantly

indicators.note: going without something means doing without it, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: the male peafowl is famous for its showy tail
taken as written: physical education

explanation.surface: A show-off boy defiantly skips his gym lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: PE is physical education, the school gym lesson.
explanation.definitionFit: Acock means cocked up, at a jaunty or defiant angle, like a hat worn with a challenging air.

clue.text: Worshipper head to foot in floral garland

indicators.note: the head letter is moved down to the foot of the word

parts.note: a toran is an Indian decoration of flowers or leaves hung over a doorway

explanation.surface: A devotee placed head to toe inside a wreath of flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: An orant is a figure in early Christian art shown praying with arms raised, a worshipper.

clue.text: Sails for e.g. Madras?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a ship's sails taken together, its canvas
second meaning: Madras is a light cotton fabric

explanation.walkthrough: Madras looks like the Indian city or the curry; here it is the checked cotton named after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors call the sails of a ship its cloth, and madras is one kind of woven fabric.

clue.text: It's crawling with cats: they're just below tiles

indicators.note: something crawling squirms about, so the letters move out of place

parts.note: taken as written; the 's that follows is read as 'is'
taken as written

explanation.surface: A place teeming with cats, the loft spaces just under the roof tiles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's crawling with cats' is read as 'it is crawling, together with cats'.
explanation.definitionFit: Attics are the rooms in the roof space of a house, directly beneath the roof covering.

clue.text: One playing with stones odd chap pockets left and right

indicators.note: a word that pockets something holds it inside

parts.note: a cure is old slang for an odd or eccentric person
l is the abbreviation for left
r is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A strange man is caught playing with stones and grabbing at both sides.
explanation.walkthrough: CURE pockets L, then R is added: CUR-L-E-R. 'Stones' suggests jewels or a stone-thrower; it is the sport's granite stones.
explanation.definitionFit: Curling is a sport where players slide heavy granite stones down ice towards a target, so its player is a curler.

clue.text: Large yacht as a rule requiring outlay of millions

indicators.note: an outlay is money paid out, so those letters are paid out of the word

parts.note: a maxim is a rule of conduct
m is the abbreviation for millions

explanation.surface: A big yacht, which as a rule costs millions to buy.
explanation.definitionFit: A maxi is a large ocean-racing yacht, built to the top size limit of its class.

clue.text: Enzyme from leaves covered in writing

indicators.note: something covered in another thing sits inside it

parts.note: prose is ordinary written language
tea is made from dried leaves

explanation.surface: Suggests a biochemical extracted from leaves described in some scientific text.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like a verb, but it is the noun, the leaves that make a cup of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A protease is any enzyme that breaks proteins down into smaller peptides and amino acids.

clue.text: Asian instrument: hospital inspector carries this out regularly?

parts.note: san is short for sanatorium, a hospital
an inspector regularly makes a round or tour of inspection

explanation.surface: Asks what a hospital inspector routinely does, with a musical instrument as the answer.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a little cryptic definition of TOUR, hence the question mark; SAN plus TOUR gives SANTOUR.
explanation.definitionFit: A santour or santoor is a hammered dulcimer of Iran and India, struck with light mallets.

clue.text: Line held by guitar in support

indicators.note: something held by another thing is gripped within it

parts.note: axe is musicians' slang for a guitar
l is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A guitar line played as backing support.
explanation.definitionFit: An axle is the rod on which a wheel turns, carrying and supporting the load above it.

clue.text: One treating deformities, I spared tooth that's rotten

indicators.note: a rotten tooth has broken up, so the letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A specialist relieved to have spared a decaying tooth, which suggests a dentist.
explanation.walkthrough: The tooth points the solver at a dentist or orthodontist, but the specialist here treats bones.
explanation.definitionFit: An orthopaedist is a doctor who corrects disorders and deformities of the bones and muscles.
